summary: The makers complete Aaron's garments, including gold worked into the ephod, engraved memorial stones, the breastplate, robe, linen clothing, and inscribed gold plate. The entire sanctuary project is then brought to Moses, who inspects it, finds that it follows God's commands, and blesses the people.
whyItMatters: The repeated reports of compliance culminate in an inspection of the whole completed work. After the earlier use of gold for the calf, skill and valuable materials now serve the instructions the community has received.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The final production of priestly garments in the camp and the presentation of all sanctuary work to Moses.
context.literaryForm: Detailed vestment construction with repeated compliance statements, followed by a completion inventory and blessing.

before.text: The outer altar, basin, court, and metal accounting are complete. The remaining construction report turns to the clothing needed for priestly service.

here.text: Small garment details accumulate into a declaration that all the work is finished; the full inventory is then inspected and blessed.

after.text: God gives the date and order for erecting the sanctuary, Moses assembles it, and the cloud and glory fill the completed dwelling.

outline.heading: The ephod and memorial shoulder stones
outline.note: Gold wires enter the woven fabric, and engraved names are set on the shoulders.

outline.heading: The breastplate and secure attachments
outline.note: Twelve named stones are set in four rows and the breastplate is fastened to the ephod.

outline.heading: The robe and remaining garments
outline.note: Bells, pomegranates, linen clothing, and the embroidered sash are completed.

outline.heading: The inscribed gold plate
outline.note: The holy crown bears its inscription and is attached to the turban.

outline.heading: All work brought to Moses
outline.note: The finished structure, furnishings, supplies, and garments are presented together.

outline.heading: Inspection and blessing
outline.note: Moses verifies compliance with the command and blesses the people.

keyVerses.text: They beat the gold into thin plates, and cut it into wires, to work it in with the blue, the purple, the scarlet, and the fine linen, the work of the skillful workman.
keyVerses.why: A specific manufacturing detail explains how gold becomes part of the woven garment.

keyVerses.text: Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting was finished. The children of Israel did according to all that Yahweh commanded Moses; so they did.
keyVerses.why: The many completed items are gathered into a statement of the whole work’s completion.

keyVerses.text: Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it as Yahweh had commanded. They had done so; and Moses blessed them.
keyVerses.why: Moses’ inspection leads to blessing, providing an explicit conclusion to the construction account.

questions.question: How is gold incorporated into the ephod’s fabric?
questions.answer: The makers beat it into thin plates and cut those into wires that can be worked with the colored material and linen. This unusually concrete detail helps explain the mixed textile and metal description.

questions.question: Why are the shoulder stones called memorials?
questions.answer: They are engraved with the names of the children of Israel and fixed to the ephod's shoulders. Their stated purpose keeps the people represented in the priest’s clothing as a continuing memorial.

questions.question: What does “breastplate” describe here?
questions.answer: It is the doubled square garment piece with four rows of named stones, attached by gold chains, rings, and a blue lace. Its construction is elaborate because it must remain joined to the ephod rather than hang loose.

questions.question: What prevents the breastplate from becoming loose?
questions.answer: The report traces upper chains and lower rings connecting it to the shoulder straps and woven band, then a blue lace binding ring to ring. It explicitly states that the fastening keeps the breastplate from coming loose from the ephod.

questions.question: How do sound, fabric, and inscription enter the garments?
questions.answer: Gold bells alternate with colored pomegranates around the robe; linen forms the tunics, head coverings, and trousers. The gold plate bears HOLY TO YAHWEH and is secured to the turban, so the work combines movement, bodily covering, and a written declaration.

questions.question: Why is Aaron’s priestly clothing made after his role in the calf episode?
questions.answer: Aaron made the calf earlier in Exodus 32:1–5, yet the renewed covenant is followed here by garments for his priestly service. The narrative preserves his commission through the crisis without giving a separate explanation in this chapter of how his responsibility for the calf is resolved.

questions.question: Why repeat the whole inventory after individual construction reports?
questions.answer: The items are now physically brought to Moses as a complete project, from coverings and furnishings to oil, cords, pins, and garments. The inventory supports the final claim that the whole work, not just a few central pieces, is ready for inspection.

glossary.def: The woven priestly garment with shoulder stones and a breastplate attached to it.
An engraved seal, invoked as the model for the lettering cut into stones and the gold plate.
The linen head covering to which the inscribed gold plate is fastened.
